fields.question: Why account for recoverability before pruning in ReCal?
fields.answer: Severe pruning can induce poor student states that distillation struggles to repair. Probe damage informs channel reselection toward recoverable structures instead of relying solely on later training.
fields.example: Removing a key arithmetic path may not be fixed by simply distilling longer.

fields.question: How does damage-weighted calibration differ from activation-size pruning?
fields.answer: Probe teacher states for damage, then reweight unpruned model statistics. Activation magnitude alone ignores recovery. Match target width and restoration protocol for fair comparison.
fields.example: A rare but badly damaged state can gain calibration weight.

fields.question: May ReCal drop probability outside teacher top candidates and renormalize?
fields.answer: No. Keep top events and remainder mass to estimate damage. Normalize response damage weights to unit scale; zero damage becomes uniform. Recompute selection from unpruned stats.
fields.example: Movement outside top tokens is invisible after local renormalization.

fields.question: Why measure pruning damage on a probe but reselect channels on the unpruned model?
fields.answer: Probe reveals harmed teacher states; use their damage to reweight original activations. This can avoid poor student trajectories that are hard to repair. Preserve remaining vocabulary mass in damage KL.
fields.example: Raise calibration weight on carry states harmed by the probe instead of patching already removed channels arbitrarily.

fields.question: Why switch PIVOT prompts to RL individually?
fields.answer: Students are not equally ready on all prompts. Uniform switching removes guidance too early for hard cases. Rank teacher perplexity on student replies and expand RL among low-perplexity prompts.
fields.example: Let familiar tasks explore rewards while unfamiliar ones still distill.

fields.question: Why aren't teacher perplexity and verified correctness interchangeable?
fields.answer: Perplexity measures teacher support for student wording, not task result. High support can be wrong and low support an effective novel route. It is a routing proxy.
fields.example: Teacher unfamiliarity with phrasing does not make the conclusion false.

fields.question: How turn PIVOT response scores into problem routing?
fields.answer: Exponentiate each response's mean teacher negative logp, average per prompt, standardize within batch and choose lowest via cosine proportion. Preserve separate GRPO/OPD normalizations, not token-level routing.
fields.example: Don't decide a whole question from only its easiest completion.

fields.question: Why route low-perplexity problems to RL earlier?
fields.answer: Teacher support on actual student responses indicates readiness for reward exploration. High perplexity retains supervision; aggregate by prompt and ramp RL share. This isn't a correctness or intrinsic difficulty test.
fields.example: Switch familiar teacher-supported steps sooner, while frequently divergent prompts continue distillation.

fields.question: Why recursively decompose and compose MagicBeanStalk problems?
fields.answer: All-fail hard tasks provide no advantage. Effective subproblem examples reveal dependency blueprints to synthesize new leaves and compose tasks with mixed current-policy outcomes. Valid format isn't efficacy.
fields.example: Practice manageable parts and recombine them without losing key dependencies.

fields.question: What do subproblem effectivity and target-policy Goldilocks each verify?
fields.answer: Effectivity asks if subexamples improve a student's parent success. Goldilocks requires mixed outcomes and at least one normally terminated success under target budget. One doesn't replace the other.
fields.example: An auxiliary learner may improve while target still fails every final sample.

fields.question: Can a well-formed local MBS problem be considered accepted?
fields.answer: No. Need complete correct solution, independent validation, blueprint/novelty and effectivity/Goldilocks checks. Retain real construction failures; isolated teacher diagnostics aren't acceptance.
fields.example: Valid JSON and dependencies do not rescue an unsolvable task.

fields.question: Why can't subproblem effectivity replace final Goldilocks selection?
fields.answer: Parent improvement checks decomposition on one learner. Final task must not be all-correct or all-wrong under target budget and needs normally completed correct trace. Local teacher probes don't complete recursive construction.
fields.example: Helpful subproblems for one student do not make a composed task learnable if target never solves it.

fields.question: Why drop some high-probability positive-advantage replies in GRPODropout?
fields.answer: They can oversharpen common modes. Selectively drop by entropy contribution while retaining failures. It isn't neuron dropout and doesn't refund generated rollouts.
fields.example: Reinforce fewer repeats of a common successful template.

fields.question: How does response dropout differ in cost from generating fewer replies?
fields.answer: Generate full group then filter updates; fewer samples would reduce generation and coverage, changing estimator. Less backward work isn't equal end-to-end savings.
fields.example: Using six of eight generated replies does not cost only six generations.

fields.question: Can GRPODropout keep original centered advantages after filtering?
fields.answer: No. Restore all nonpositive samples and recenter retained ones by old-policy probability. Dropping either condition changes feedback/baseline.
fields.example: Removing strong positives shifts the reference and requires recentering.

fields.question: Why filter high-probability positives but retain all nonpositives?
fields.answer: Dominant successes can further reduce entropy; select by entropy contribution, not random removal. Preserve negative learning and recenter with old probabilities. Generation cost is already paid.
fields.example: Downweight repeated successful templates without turning failures into omitted feedback.

fields.question: Why multiply DIAL-OPD log gaps by logarithmic probability mean?
fields.answer: Tokens near impossible under both models can have large log differences. Scaling downweights such noise and prioritizes supported disagreements. Selection is not verifier truth.
fields.example: A bizarre word differing tenfold may matter less than a small gap on a key digit.

fields.question: How does sparse DIAL supervision differ from deleting unselected text?
fields.answer: Unselected tokens stay as context but have masked losses. Removing text changes later prefixes and teacher scores.
fields.example: Keep preceding arithmetic/connectives even when not training their tokens.

fields.question: How handle equal p and q in DIAL's logarithmic mean?
fields.answer: Use its continuous limit. Choose each response's own valid-position quota, detach advantages and differentiate final student logp only. Global ranking can let long answers dominate.
fields.example: Equal probabilities have a finite limit, not NaN or an arbitrary large score.

fields.question: Why not select solely by largest teacher–student logp gaps?
fields.answer: Huge gaps can occur in negligible mass. Logarithmic probability mean rescales priorities. Keep masked tokens as context; sparse supervision does not reduce generation or prove errors.
fields.example: An unlikely odd word should not drown out disagreement on a realistic key step.

fields.question: Why use output-layer gradients as LESSER selection features?
fields.answer: Full per-example backprop is costly. Independent readout gradient follows analytically from prediction residual and final hidden state in one forward, then project for the existing selector.
fields.example: Keep query similarity selection but replace expensive gradient features.

fields.question: Is LESSER fully equivalent to full-model gradient similarity?
fields.answer: No. Exactness applies to an independent output layer; tied embeddings add hidden-state paths. Projection also approximates geometry and downstream performance needs testing.
fields.example: Similar final-layer directions do not guarantee similar middle-layer updates.

fields.question: Why share random projections between LESSER candidates and queries?
fields.answer: Only shared coordinates support comparison. Project both residual and hidden sides without materializing the full outer product. Use validation query proxies, never test selection; local random tensors are diagnostics.
fields.example: Independent projection draws per sample destroy comparability.

fields.question: Why isn't one-forward analytic output gradient an exact full-model substitute?
fields.answer: The outer product is exact for an independent readout; shared bilateral projection compresses it for existing selection. Tied embeddings can introduce indirect gradients. Use validation proxies and isolate test. This is not all-layer gradient equality.
fields.example: Select training examples using readout gradients of validation queries, not test examples.
